headline: Tiniest Porpoise Gets Digital Lifeline as Species Faces Extinction
meta_description: Researchers create detailed 3D digital models of a rare vaquita skeleton, preserving knowledge of Earth's smallest and most endangered porpoise.
summary_short: Scientists have digitally preserved a vaquita skeleton using advanced imaging, creating a permanent record of the world's rarest porpoise before it vanishes.
body:
The vaquita porpoise, the world's smallest cetacean at just 5 feet long, exists in the wild only in Mexico's Gulf of California—and its population has dwindled to as few as ten individuals. Now, researchers from Florida Atlantic University, working with the San Diego Natural History Museum, SeaWorld California, and NOAA Fisheries, have created a detailed digital archive of a rare vaquita skeleton that offers both scientific insight and a glimmer of hope. Using medical CT scanning, high-resolution micro-CT imaging, and digital photography, the team transformed a specimen donated to the museum in 1966 into precise 3D models that can be studied without handling the fragile original bone.

The vaquita's decline stems largely from entanglement in illegal gillnets intended for other banned species destined for the black market. Known for the striking dark rings around its eyes and mouth, this porpoise only became recognized by science in the latter half of the 20th century—yet it already faces the brink of extinction. The new digital project, published in June 2026 in Marine Mammal Science, makes all data freely available through the open-access repository MorphoSource, including photographs, scan data, and downloadable 3D models.

What makes this effort especially powerful is its scope. Researchers and educators worldwide can now access detailed skeletal information for a species most will never see alive. Museums and classrooms can create 3D-printed replicas for learning; scientists can study microscopic bone detail to understand the species better; conservation efforts gain a permanent reference point. By transforming one fragile specimen into a shareable digital permanent record, the team has ensured that knowledge of the vaquita survives even if the animal itself does not. Meanwhile, urgent international efforts are already underway to eliminate gillnet fishing in vaquita habitat—a race against time that this digital legacy now supports.
quick_facts: Vaquita population: fewer than ten individuals remaining in the wild
Size: world's smallest cetacean at 5 feet long
Location: Gulf of California (Sea of Cortez), Mexico only
Skeleton digitized using medical CT and micro-CT imaging technology
All 3D data freely available through MorphoSource repository
